issues.subcategory: Confounded perceptual vs. memory illusion logic
issues.description: The core logic for distinguishing perceptual from memory illusions relies on illusions increasing over time. However, this logic is incomplete: if perceptual illusions occur on some trials and memory illusions on others, the total rate would still increase over time even if the memory component were absent. More critically, the authors never directly measure perception at time zero (immediately at stimulus offset before any delay), so the baseline perceptual illusion rate is never established. The argument that 'if illusions were purely perceptual they should not increase over time' is valid only if all perceptual illusions are immediately encoded as such—but if perceptual encoding itself takes time (e.g., consolidation during the blank interval), illusions could increase even without a memory component.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding. After all, at both time points initial perceptual processing was finished, so if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time.

issues.subcategory: No zero-delay / immediate perception baseline condition
issues.description: To properly separate perceptual from memory illusions, a condition probing participants at or near stimulus offset (e.g., 0 ms or <100 ms delay) is needed to establish the baseline perceptual illusion rate. The shortest delay used is 500–750 ms, which is already well beyond iconic memory duration and into the fragile/working memory range. Without a true perceptual baseline, the claim that illusions 'increase from perception' cannot be fully substantiated.
issues.quote: In all experiments participants see memory displays that contain both real letters, with the standard orientation, and pseudo-letters, which were mirrored... These experiments test whether STM is susceptible to illusory memories, even when the visual information has only just disappeared, and the perceptual memory trace should still be intact

issues.subcategory: Confound between memory delay and interference conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the three conditions conflate two distinct manipulations: temporal delay (Short 0.75s vs. Long 3s) and visual interference (Short vs. Short-with-interference). These are treated as a single 'Memory Delay' factor with three levels, but they manipulate different mechanisms (decay vs. interference). Combining them into one factor makes it impossible to cleanly attribute the increase in illusions to either decay or interference specifically, and the theoretical interpretation shifts between the two throughout the paper.
issues.quote: The experiment had three memory conditions. In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display. If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition).

issues.subcategory: Contradictory numbers in Experiment 1 results
issues.description: The Results section states illusory errors increase '7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay.' However, the Discussion of Experiment 1 states 'From the Short... to the Long condition... or the Short with interference... the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%.' These figures (19% vs. 29% for the Short condition) are inconsistent within the same experiment. The Results section appears to report overall (collapsed across target types) while the Discussion reports pseudo-letter targets only, but this is not made explicit and creates confusion.
issues.quote: the increase in illusory errors (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay)... From the Short (memory probe 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display with no visual interference) to the Long condition (memory probe after 3 seconds) or the Short with interference (memory probe after .75 seconds following an interfering display) the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%, respectively.

issues.subcategory: Figure reference error in Experiment 4
issues.description: The Results section of Experiment 4 states 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials,' but Figure 5 is the figure for Experiment 3. Experiment 4's figure is labeled Figure 6 in the manuscript. This is a clear internal inconsistency in figure referencing.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent BFincl reporting for Table 4
issues.description: Table 4 (Follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory error rates in Experiment 2) reports BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay, yet the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay).' These values are contradictory by several orders of magnitude. One of these values must be erroneous. This is a critical statistical reporting error that undermines the interpretation of non-illusory error patterns.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets

issues.subcategory: Misidentified BFincl in Table 1 text
issues.description: The text reports 'BFincl = 4.21' for the Memory Delay * Error Type interaction in Experiment 1, which matches Table 1 (BFincl = 4.205). However, the text also states 'BFincl>1000' for both Error Type and Target Type * Error Type, while Table 1 shows these as 1.462e+14 and 8.871e+14 respectively. While technically '>1000' is correct, reporting '>1000' for values of 10^14 obscures the actual magnitude and is inconsistent with the precision used for other values (e.g., 4.21). This selective precision in reporting inflates the apparent contrast between effects.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 was supported: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000).

issues.subcategory: Unequal trial proportions creating response bias
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the target was a real letter in 75% of trials and a pseudo-letter in only 25% of trials. This creates a strong base-rate bias toward selecting real letters, which could directly produce the asymmetry in pseudo-to-real vs. real-to-pseudo illusions that is attributed to 'world knowledge.' While Experiments 3 and 4 address this with balanced stimuli, the authors' interpretation of Experiments 1 and 2 as evidence for world knowledge is weakened by this confound, and the authors acknowledge it only partially.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in 75% of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining 25%... It is important to note, though, that throughout the experiment participants were more likely to encounter real letters as the target, and as the correct response option, than pseudo-letters

issues.subcategory: Participant exclusion based on confidence rates creates selection bias
issues.description: Participants with fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in any cell were excluded. In Experiment 1, this excluded 5 of 40 participants (12.5%); in Experiment 2, 92 of 290 (32%) were excluded. Excluded participants had systematically lower confidence rates (26.2% vs. 53.8% in Exp. 1; 15.7% vs. 49.2% in Exp. 2). This exclusion criterion is not pre-registered and creates a systematic selection bias: participants who rarely express high confidence—potentially those who are more cautious or have better metacognition—are excluded, leaving a sample biased toward overconfident responders who are more likely to show the illusion effect.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)... Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions

issues.subcategory: Confidence scale inconsistency across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 1 used a 2-point confidence scale (1=guess, 2=certain), while Experiments 2, 3, and 4 used a 4-point scale (1-4). This makes direct quantitative comparison of 'high confidence' responses across experiments problematic. The threshold for 'high confidence' is not defined consistently, and the different scales may capture different psychological states. This is not acknowledged as a limitation when comparing results across experiments.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain)... then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4)

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc collapse over cue color condition without pre-registration
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the cue color manipulation (testing transiently induced expectations) was a primary hypothesis. When it failed to show an effect, the authors collapsed over cue color conditions for all subsequent analyses. This decision was made post-hoc based on the null result, which is a form of analytic flexibility. If the cue color had shown an effect, it would presumably have been retained as a factor. The decision rule for collapsing is not pre-specified.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors... The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that the best model only contained a main effect of target type... Because of this, in subsequent analyses all data are collapsed over the two cue types (red and blue).

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration for Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 do not mention any pre-registration. Only Experiments 3 and 4 describe a sequential Bayes Factor stopping rule. The absence of pre-registration for the first two experiments means that the exclusion criteria, the choice of which interactions to test, the decision to use Bayesian ANOVA, and the model selection procedure could all have been determined after data collection, introducing undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test

issues.subcategory: Different stopping rules across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 3 used a BF stopping threshold of 6, while Experiment 4 used a threshold of 10. These different thresholds are not justified, and the choice of threshold affects both the final sample size and the strength of evidence claimed. Using different thresholds across experiments that are meant to replicate and extend each other introduces inconsistency in the evidentiary standard.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop... once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Online data collection in Experiment 4 without equivalence testing
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Neurotask/Zoom, while Experiments 1-3 were conducted in-person in controlled laboratory settings. Online experiments introduce uncontrolled variability in display timing, screen calibration, viewing distance, ambient lighting, and distraction. The authors do not test for equivalence between online and lab conditions, nor do they acknowledge this as a potential confound when comparing results across experiments.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.subcategory: Irrelevant second display timing confound
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the irrelevant second display appears at different times relative to the memory probe depending on condition: in the Short condition it appears 3.75s after the probe, in the Long condition 1.5s after the probe, and in the Short-with-interference condition simultaneously with the probe. This means the second display's temporal relationship to the probe—not just its presence—varies across conditions, making it impossible to isolate the effect of interference from the effect of the second display's timing on memory consolidation.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5s (Long delay) or 3.75s (short delay).

issues.subcategory: Causal claims about world knowledge from correlational design
issues.description: The authors claim that 'world knowledge' drives STM illusions based on the asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors. However, this asymmetry could also result from differential perceptual discriminability (pseudo-letters may be harder to discriminate from real letters than vice versa due to asymmetric familiarity effects on perceptual processing), differential encoding strength, or response bias. The design does not include a manipulation that directly varies world knowledge (e.g., training participants on pseudo-letters to make them equally familiar), so the causal attribution to world knowledge remains inferential.
issues.quote: The interaction between Target Type and Error Type (BFincl >1000) provides evidence for Hypothesis 3: when the target is a pseudo-letter, illusions are very common (37%) but other errors occur much less often (11%)... This suggests that world knowledge is a more important driver of illusory memories than visual similarity

issues.subcategory: Predictive processing framework not uniquely supported
issues.description: The authors claim their results 'support a predictive processing view' of STM. However, the results are equally consistent with multiple alternative frameworks (signal detection theory with asymmetric priors, fuzzy trace theory with asymmetric gist strength, simple response bias, or differential encoding). The authors briefly discuss FTT but dismiss it without a decisive empirical test. The predictive processing framework is not uniquely supported by the data—it is one of several compatible accounts.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions, such that prior expectations can shape memory traces.

issues.subcategory: Operationalization of 'high confidence' as illusion criterion
issues.description: The authors use high-confidence errors as the defining criterion for 'memory illusions' to distinguish them from guesses. However, high confidence in an error could also reflect a strong response bias (e.g., always confidently selecting real letters regardless of memory content), a metacognitive miscalibration, or a perceptual illusion that was confidently encoded. The confidence rating alone does not validate that the participant had an actual (false) memory trace as opposed to a confident guess or a confident perceptual error. No validation of the confidence measure as an index of memory trace presence is provided.
issues.quote: Isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: STM vs. working memory vs. fragile memory conflation
issues.description: The paper claims to study 'STM illusions' but the experimental delays (0.5s to 3s) span multiple theoretically distinct memory systems (iconic memory, fragile memory, working memory). The authors acknowledge this in the General Discussion but treat results from all delays as evidence for a unified 'STM illusion' phenomenon. The theoretical implications differ substantially depending on which memory system is implicated, and the paper does not provide conditions that cleanly isolate each system.
issues.quote: Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.subcategory: Missing raw accuracy data and d-prime measures
issues.description: The paper reports only error rates on high-confidence trials, not overall accuracy, d-prime, or criterion measures. Without overall accuracy data, it is impossible to assess whether the high-confidence error rates are inflated by generally poor performance, or to evaluate the relationship between memory sensitivity and illusion rates. Signal detection theory measures would be essential for properly characterizing the memory illusion phenomenon.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on how 'high confidence' was defined for analysis
issues.description: In Experiments 2-4, a 4-point confidence scale was used, but the paper never specifies which confidence levels were classified as 'high confidence' for the primary analyses. It is unclear whether only level 4 was used, levels 3-4, or some other threshold. This is critical information for replication and for interpreting the results.
issues.quote: After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.subcategory: Appendix 1 referenced but not provided
issues.description: Throughout the results sections, full model comparisons are said to be in 'Appendix 1,' but this appendix does not appear in the manuscript as provided. Without the full model comparison tables, readers cannot evaluate the model selection procedure or verify the reported BFm values.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 1 for an overview of BFincl for each model component

issues.subcategory: Missing prior specification for Bayesian analyses
issues.description: The Bayesian ANOVAs are conducted in JASP but the prior distributions used (e.g., Cauchy scale parameter for effect sizes, prior model probabilities) are not reported. Different prior specifications can substantially change Bayes Factors, especially for moderate effects. Without this information, the analyses cannot be reproduced or critically evaluated.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type.

issues.subcategory: No effect size measures reported
issues.description: No effect size measures (e.g., partial eta-squared, Cohen's d, posterior distributions of effect sizes) are reported for any of the four experiments. Bayes Factors indicate evidence for effects but do not convey effect magnitude. Without effect sizes, the practical significance of the illusions cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 was supported: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000).

issues.subcategory: High exclusion rate in Experiment 2 not adequately addressed
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded due to insufficient high-confidence trials. This is a very high exclusion rate that substantially reduces statistical power and introduces selection bias. The authors note that excluded participants had lower confidence rates but do not analyze whether excluded participants differed on other relevant variables (age, performance accuracy, etc.), nor do they conduct sensitivity analyses with the full sample.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion for missing cells without sensitivity analysis
issues.description: In Experiment 3, one additional participant was excluded from the main ANOVA due to listwise deletion caused by zero high-confidence responses in one or more cells. The authors do not report how many cells had zero responses for other participants, whether imputation was considered, or whether the results are robust to this exclusion.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: WEIRD sample and student population
issues.description: All experiments used university student samples (primarily first-year psychology students) from the University of Amsterdam. The illusion effects are attributed to 'world knowledge' about letters acquired through lifelong exposure to the alphabet. However, the degree of letter familiarity, reading habits, and metacognitive strategies may vary substantially across cultures, ages, and educational backgrounds. The generalizability of the findings to non-student, non-Western, or less literate populations is not discussed.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: Overclaim about all STM stages
issues.description: The abstract and conclusion claim that 'all memory stages, including STM' are susceptible to illusions. However, the authors explicitly acknowledge that iconic memory was not tested. The claim about 'all stages' is therefore not supported by the data.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions

issues.subcategory: Generalization from letters to all visual percepts
issues.description: The General Discussion extrapolates from letter-specific illusions to 'visual percepts in general,' citing the Chalk et al. motion study. Letters are a highly overlearned, culturally specific category with strong categorical representations. The mechanisms driving letter illusions may not generalize to other visual categories. This extrapolation is speculative and not supported by the current data.
issues.quote: Secondly, it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general. This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.

issues.subcategory: Dismissal of FTT without adequate empirical test
issues.description: The authors dismiss Fuzzy Trace Theory (FTT) by arguing it predicts that high similarity between target and lure should facilitate false memories, which they claim is inconsistent with their data because pseudo-letters and real letters are 'extremely similar.' However, FTT's similarity prediction refers to semantic/conceptual similarity, not visual similarity. Pseudo-letters and real letters are visually similar but semantically distinct (one is a letter, one is not). The authors misapply FTT's similarity principle, making their dismissal of FTT logically flawed.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of De Gardelle et al. findings
issues.description: The authors repeatedly claim that De Gardelle et al. (2009) interpreted their results as perceptual illusions and 'did not explore the possibility that their results could be due to memory errors.' However, the current paper's own paradigm is directly adapted from De Gardelle et al., and the authors use the same WM probe methodology. If De Gardelle et al.'s paradigm is susceptible to memory illusions, so is the current paradigm at the shortest delay. The authors cannot simultaneously use De Gardelle et al.'s paradigm as their model and critique it for not distinguishing perception from memory.
issues.quote: De Gardelle and colleagues (2009) conclude that this reflects a perceptual illusion – in other words that their participants make an incorrect perceptual inference at the time of perception. They did not explore the possibility that their results could be due to memory errors instead of perceptual errors.

issues.subcategory: Training task uses different stimuli than main experiment
issues.description: The training task in Experiment 1 uses oriented rectangles (bars), while the main experiment uses letters. The training is designed to ensure participants can perform the cued change detection task, but the transfer of skills from bar orientation discrimination to letter identity discrimination is not validated. Participants who pass the bar training threshold may still perform poorly on letter discrimination, and the 75% threshold may not be appropriate for the letter task.
issues.quote: Prior to the main experiment, participants were trained on a cued change detection task. In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.subcategory: Absence of awareness check for cue-target contingency in Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the color of the fixation cross was associated with pseudo-letter target probability (25% for red, 60% for blue). Participants completed a post-experiment questionnaire, and the authors report that 'the relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.' However, the questionnaire content and scoring criteria are not described, making it impossible to evaluate whether awareness was adequately assessed. Participants may have had partial awareness that did not reach explicit report.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: Unbalanced response display in Experiment 1 may drive asymmetry
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display included the pseudo-letter counterpart on only 50% of pseudo-letter target trials, but the real letter counterpart on only 16% of real-letter target trials. This means participants had more opportunities to select the real letter counterpart when the target was a pseudo-letter than vice versa, which could directly produce the pseudo-to-real asymmetry attributed to world knowledge. While Experiment 2 addresses this by always including both, the interpretation of Experiment 1's asymmetry as evidence for world knowledge is confounded.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent description of Experiment 3 discussion referencing Experiment 1-3
issues.description: The Discussion of Experiment 3 states 'participants still show the same pattern of results as observed in Experiment 1-3,' but Experiment 3 is the experiment being discussed. This should read 'Experiment 1-2,' as Experiment 3 cannot be used to validate itself.
issues.quote: when letters and pseudo-letters are just as prevalent, participants still show the same pattern of results as observed in Experiment 1-3, with a stronger tendency to report, with high confidence, that they have seen a real letter

issues.subcategory: Missing information about letter set used
issues.description: The paper states that symmetrical letters (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) were excluded, but does not specify which letters from the remaining asymmetric set were actually used in the experiments. The specific letter identities could affect results (e.g., some pseudo-letters may be more confusable with real letters than others, or some letters may have stronger memory representations). This information is necessary for replication.
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays).

issues.subcategory: No inter-experiment reliability or replication statistics reported
issues.description: The paper presents four experiments as converging evidence but does not report any formal cross-experiment replication statistics (e.g., meta-analytic Bayes Factors, effect size comparisons across experiments). The claim of 'consistent' replication is made qualitatively without quantitative support, making it difficult to assess whether effect sizes are stable across the different methodological variations.
issues.quote: Four experiments consistently show that illusory memories can arise even when the to-be-remembered items have only just disappeared from vision.
